title: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)
hook: blessed in the city and the field, coming in and going out
tomorrow: Ki Tavo: a heart to know (Deuteronomy 29:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ki Tavo, hayom: the old commandments, new each day. Your line was this day, new. What did you notice in something familiar? Today, blessings for every step of an ordinary day. Day five hundred fifteen.

Count how many thresholds you'll cross today. Out the front door. Into a car or onto a bus. Into work, or school, or a store. Back out. Back home. Most of those crossings take less than a second and leave no memory at all. In many Jewish homes, the doorframe holds a small case, a mezuzah, and people touch it as they pass, going in and going out. The doorway is treated as a place worth a moment. Today's verses bless exactly those crossings, and everything around them.
screen: `COUNT THE DOORWAYS.` → `A HAND ON THE MEZUZAH.` → `THE CROSSINGS, BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy twenty-eight opens with a list of blessings, if the people keep the covenant. It starts small and wide at the same time: "Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field." Then the children and the herds, the basket and the kneading-trough. And it ends: "Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out." City and field cover where you are. Coming in and going out cover how you move between them. Between the two, hardly a moment of the day is left out. The basket and the kneading-trough are kitchen things, where the bread begins. The blessing reaches right into the bowl. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, gives the last verse a second reading. Coming in and going out, it says, can mean coming into the world and leaving it: may your leaving be like your arriving, free of wrongdoing. A whole life read as one doorway. A psalm uses the same pair: "The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever." These blessings sit in a hard chapter. They're short, and the curses that follow are long and frightening; by custom the reader chants those quickly and in a lowered voice. But the chapter begins with blessing, and the blessing is about the most ordinary movements a person makes.
screen: `IN THE CITY, IN THE FIELD.` · `THE BASKET AND THE KNEADING-TROUGH.` · `ARRIVING IN, AND LEAVING, THE WORLD.` · `SHORT BLESSINGS, A HARD CHAPTER.` · then, large: `BLESSED COMING AND GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless your leaving and your returning. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door you'll walk out of next. See your hand on it. Before you go through, imagine pausing for half a second. If you pray, the psalm's words are there: the LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in. If you don't, a breath and a wish that the day goes well will do. Now picture coming back through the same door tonight. Pause there too. Two thresholds, two small moments, kept. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion where blessing covers the city and the field, the coming in and the going out.
Your line: blessed coming and going. Today, at one door, pause for a breath as you leave, and another as you come back. Day five hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Many Jews touch the mezuzah on the doorframe when entering and leaving a home, and Psalm 121, with its line about going out and coming in, is often said before a journey.

fork.setup: you're the Torah reader in synagogue, and you've reached the long curses of chapter 28. what does custom say?
options: chant them quickly, in a lowered voice.
fork.reveal: they're read, not skipped, but quickly and quietly, while the blessings that open the chapter are read in full voice.

original.note: Hebrew: blessed are you in your coming in. Deuteronomy 28:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice wish for travelers.
what it means: blessing reaches every crossing of the day, and the whole of a life from arriving to leaving.
what a scholar hears: Bava Metzia 107a reads 28:6 as entering and leaving the world without sin; the pair returns in Psalm 121:8.

sources.quoted: Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field.
Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out.
The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever.
